ta-l3d23q2-d1e108.summary: Prooemium to the second question of Distinction 23, which turns from virtue in general to faith in particular. It lists five articles: what faith is, its act, its subject, whether it is a virtue, and its order to the other virtues.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e120.summary: First objection to the Apostle's definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1 ('the substance of things to be hoped for, the argument of things not appearing'): no habit is a substance, and faith is a habit, so faith is not a substance.
claims: Faith, being a habit, cannot be called a substance.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e131.summary: Second objection: a definition should be given from what is prior and per se, and the per se object of faith is the thing to be believed, not hoped for, since hope comes after faith. So the definition should say 'things to be believed'.
claims: The definition should name faith's per se object, things to be believed, not things to be hoped for.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e134.summary: Third objection: charity follows faith as hope does and is closer to the end than hope. So the definition should rather say 'substance of things to be loved'.
claims: Since charity is nearer the end than hope, faith should be defined by reference to things loved.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e138.summary: Fourth objection: faith concerns what is above reason, while argument is an act of reason. So faith is not an argument.
claims: Faith, being above reason, cannot be an argument, which is an act of reason.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e141.summary: Fifth objection: the same thing should not be placed in different genera, and argument and substance are different genera. So defining faith by both is faulty.
claims: Defining faith by both substance and argument puts it in two genera.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e144.summary: Sixth objection: things that are true but not apparent are doubtful. Since faith is a kind of knowledge, the definition should say 'of doubtful things' rather than 'of things not appearing'.
claims: Truths not apparent are doubtful, so faith should be described as of doubtful things.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e147.summary: Seventh objection: knowledge precedes affection, but the definition places 'substance of things hoped for' (affection) before 'argument of things not appearing' (knowledge). So its parts are badly ordered.
claims: Since cognition precedes affection, the cognitive part of the definition should come first.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e156.summary: Eighth objection: one thing has one definition as it has one being, yet many other definitions of faith are given. So this one seems insufficient.
claims: The multiplicity of definitions of faith shows this one is insufficient.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e159.summary: Aquinas's determination: the Apostle's statement is a correct and proper definition of faith as regards what a definition requires, though not in the formal manner of a definition, which authors and philosophers often neglect, as they omit syllogistic form while supplying its materials. A habit is known through its act, an act is specified by its object and has goodness from its end. So the Apostle defines faith by its object, the thing not appearing (not apparent to natural knowledge), and by its end, the substance of things to be hoped for. God is both object and end of faith but under different rationes: as object, he is first truth beyond our natural intellect, hence 'not appearing'; as end, he is a good that exceeds human capacity yet communicates itself out of liberality, hence 'thing to be hoped for'.
claims: The Apostle's description of faith is a true definition in content, though not in formal shape.
Faith is defined through its object and its end, because a habit is known through its act, which is specified by object and made good by end.
God is the object of faith as first truth exceeding natural intellect, and its end as a good exceeding human power yet freely communicable.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e166.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith is called substance not as belonging to that category but because it shares a property of substance. As substance is the foundation of all other beings, faith is the foundation of the whole spiritual edifice, as light is called the hypostasis of colour.
claims: Faith is called substance because it is the foundation of the spiritual life.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e169.summary: Reply to the second objection: 'things to be hoped for' names faith's end, not its object. The ultimate end of faith is the truth whose vision replaces faith, but truth as such does not express the ratio of end; hope, as a movement toward the end, names its terminus. In habits pertaining to the will, the end is first in intention though last in attainment.
claims: 'Things to be hoped for' names the end of faith, not its object.
The end is first in intention though last in attainment.
concepts: hope as motion to the end

ta-l3d23q2-d1e175.summary: Reply to the third objection: love concerns both what is possessed and what is to be attained, but hope only what is to be attained (Romans 8:24). Since faith concerns what is unseen, 'things to be hoped for' expresses the end proper to the state in which faith exists, and definitions must be given from what is proper.
claims: Hope, being only of what is not yet possessed, expresses faith's relation to its end more properly than love.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e184.summary: Reply to the fourth objection, by distinguishing senses of 'argumentum'. Properly it is reason's process from known to unknown, or 'a reason producing belief in a doubtful matter' (Boethius). By extension it names the middle term, any brief foretaste of a later narrative (as the argumenta prefixed to Paul's letters), and the light by which principles are made manifest. Faith is an argument in the last three senses: as manifesting other things (one article manifesting another, theological conclusions drawn from articles, one person's faith confirming another's); as a foretaste of future vision; and as an infused light manifesting the articles, as the agent intellect's light manifests first principles. The first of these is accidental to faith, so the definition uses one of the latter two.
claims: 'Argumentum' can mean reasoning, its middle term, a foretaste of what follows, or the light that manifests principles.
Faith is an argument as a foretaste of future vision and as an infused light manifesting the articles.
That faith manifests other truths or confirms others' faith is accidental to it.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e187.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: 'argument' and 'substance' are not placed in the definition as genera but as acts, since habits are customarily defined by acts. One expresses faith's relation to its object, the other its relation to its ultimate end.
claims: Substance and argument function in the definition as acts, not genera.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e190.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: doubt removes firmness of adherence, which 'not appearing' does not; it only removes vision of the thing believed. Faith has firm adherence but not full vision, so it is of things not appearing, not of doubtful things.
claims: Faith lacks vision but not firmness of adherence, so it is not of doubtful things.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e194.summary: Reply to the seventh objection: the knowledge of faith proceeds from the will, since no one believes unless willing. So it is fitting that what pertains to affection comes first in the definition.
claims: Because belief proceeds from the will, the affective part of the definition may rightly come first.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e197.summary: Reply to the eighth objection: a definition comprehending all the principles of a thing would be unique, but definitions differ when they include some principles and omit others. The Apostle's definition includes end, object and act, and from these subject and genus can be inferred (the act reveals the power, the remote genus habit, and the end the proximate genus virtue). Aquinas then shows how other definitions reduce to it: Damascene's (which adds the accident of certainty), Dionysius's 'abiding foundation of believers', Augustine's 'virtue by which unseen things are believed', Damascene's 'non-inquisitive consent', and Hugh of St Victor's 'certainty about absent things above opinion and below science', which is derivable from 'argument' (certainty) and 'not appearing' (absence). The Apostle's definition includes all the others.
claims: Definitions of one thing vary when they express different subsets of its principles.
The Apostle's definition includes end, object and act, from which subject and genus follow.
The definitions of Damascene, Dionysius, Augustine and Hugh of St Victor are all contained in the Apostle's.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e248.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is believing 'to think with assent', as Augustine says?): assenting, like consenting, belongs to the will, while believing belongs to cognition. So believing is not assenting.
claims: Assent belongs to the will, while belief is cognitive.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e251.summary: Second objection: thinking (cogitare, 'co-agitate') implies inquiry, but faith is a 'non-inquisitive consent' (Damascene). So believing is assent without thought rather than with it.
claims: Faith excludes inquiry and so excludes cogitatio.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e254.summary: Third objection: thinking is the act of the cogitative power, which philosophers place in the sensitive part with a determinate organ, while matters of faith are grasped by the intellect alone. So believing involves no cogitation.
claims: Cogitation is a sensitive act and so cannot belong to faith, which is intellectual.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e257.summary: Fourth objection: if believing is thinking with assent, so is knowing scientifically; so knowing would be the same as believing, which is false.
claims: The description fits scientia as well as faith and so fails to define belief.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e266.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (are the acts of faith rightly multiplied as believing God, believing God's word, and believing in God?): one habit has one act, so only one act should be assigned to faith.
claims: One habit has only one act.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e269.summary: Second objection: what is demonstrated is matter of science, not faith, and that God exists is demonstrated even by philosophers. So believing that God exists is not an act of faith.
claims: God's existence is demonstrable and so not an object of faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e272.summary: Third objection: the act of faith distinguishes believer from unbeliever, yet even unbelievers hold that God speaks only truth. So the act of faith is rather believing God's messenger, and believing a human is more an act of faith than believing God.
claims: Since everyone grants that God speaks truly, faith must consist in believing the human messenger.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e275.summary: Fourth objection: faith and charity are distinct virtues, and loving God is the act of charity. So 'loving by believing' is not an act of faith.
claims: Love belongs to charity, not to faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e279.summary: Fifth objection: by loving God one tends to him, adheres to him and is incorporated into his members, so Lombard's piling up of these phrases is superfluous.
claims: The fourfold description of believing in God is redundant.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e288.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (is faith less certain than science?): Hugh of St Victor says faith is a certainty about absent things below science and above opinion. So faith is less certain than science.
claims: Faith ranks below science in certainty.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e291.summary: Second objection: what is less mixed with doubt is more certain. Scientific knowledge admits no doubt, while belief admits some movement of doubt while faith remains. So faith is less certain than science.
claims: Faith admits movements of doubt that science excludes.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e294.summary: Third objection: all certainty arises from sense or intellectual vision, and faith concerns what is seen by neither. So faith has no certainty.
claims: Certainty derives from vision, which faith lacks.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e297.summary: Sed contra: Augustine says nothing is more certain to a person than their faith.
claims: Nothing is more certain to a person than their faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e301.summary: Second sed contra: faith is more certain as the reason producing it is firmer. Human reason, which produces science, falls infinitely short of the divine reason that produces faith. So faith is far more certain than science.
claims: Because faith rests on divine reason, it is more certain than science, which rests on human reason.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e311.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1, a central analysis of the act of belief. The intellect has two operations: simple apprehension of quiddities, where there is no truth or falsity and hence no assent, and composition and division, where truth and falsity arise and the intellect assents or dissents. Faith, as assent, belongs to the second. Assent determines the intellect to one side of a contradiction, which happens in three ways. Considered in itself, the intellect is determined by the presence of the intelligible, as with first principles (understanding, also called vision). Ordered to reason, it is determined when conclusions are resolved into self-evident principles (science). Ordered to the will, it is determined by the will's command to adhere to what is neither seen nor resolvable into what is seen, because the will judges it good to adhere for some reason, though that reason is insufficient to terminate the intellect. This is believing, and it is why faith is said to captivate the intellect. Where the reason suffices neither for intellect nor will, one has opinion, accepting one side with fear of the other. Where reasons are absent or balanced, there is ignorance or doubt. So 'to think with assent' uniquely identifies the believer: the one who understands has assent without cogitation, the one who knows scientifically has cogitation before assent, the believer has assent together with cogitation (since the intellect, not terminated in itself, keeps moving), the one who opines has cogitation with imperfect assent, the doubter cogitation without assent, and the ignorant neither.
claims: Faith belongs to the intellect's second operation, composition and division, where assent is possible.
The intellect is determined to one side of a contradiction by evidence (understanding), by resolution to principles (science), or by the will's command (belief).
In belief, reason determines the intellect only through the will, which is why faith is said to captivate the intellect.
Opinion holds one side with fear of the other; doubt and ignorance involve no assent.
The believer alone has assent and cogitation together, because the intellect is determined from outside, by the will, while remaining restless in itself.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e314.summary: Reply to the first objection: since sense does not compare but receives one thing determinately, the determination even of higher powers is named from sensing. The determination of cogitation is called assent (ad-sentire), since nothing precedes it; the will's determination is called consent (con-sentire), since it presupposes cogitation with which it 'feels together' as it tends to what reason judges good. So consent belongs to the will and assent to the intellect.
claims: Assent is the intellect's determination and consent the will's.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e317.summary: Reply to the second objection: Damascene's 'non-inquisitive' excludes the inquiry of reason that would terminate the intellect, not the inquiry that inclines the will. Since the intellect is not terminated, it retains a motion toward its own determination. So faith lies between two cogitations: one that precedes faith and inclines the will to believe, and one that accompanies assent and tends toward understanding what is already believed, as in Isaiah 7:9, 'unless you believe, you will not understand'.
claims: Faith excludes inquiry that terminates the intellect but not inquiry that inclines the will.
Faith stands between a preceding cogitation that inclines the will and a concomitant cogitation that seeks understanding of what is believed.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e328.summary: Reply to the third objection: the cogitative power lies on the border of sense and intellect, considering particular forms like sense and comparing like intellect, and so exists only in humans. Since sense is better known than intellect, all intellectual comparing is named 'cogitation' from it.
claims: The cogitative power lies at the border of sense and intellect, and intellectual comparison is named from it.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e332.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: it is clear from the solution that the description belongs only to the believer.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e341.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: the believer's act depends on three things, the intellect determined to one, the will that determines it by command, and the reason that inclines the will. Hence three acts are named. As the intellect is terminated, the act is 'believing God' (credere Deum), since faith's object is God himself or something about or from him. As the intellect is determined by the will, it is 'believing in God' (credere in Deum), tending to him by love. As reason inclines the will, it is 'believing God' as witness (credere Deo), since the will is moved to assent to what it does not see because God says it, as one believes the testimony of a good person who sees what one does not.
claims: The act of belief depends on intellect, will and reason, yielding credere Deum, credere in Deum and credere Deo.
The reason that inclines the will to believe is that God says it, on the model of trusting a reliable witness.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e344.summary: Reply to the first objection: all three names denote one complete act of faith, named in different ways from the different factors in faith; in the act by which one believes in God, one also believes God and believes God's word.
claims: The three formulas name one complete act of faith under different aspects.
concepts: unity of the act of faith

ta-l3d23q2-d1e347.summary: Reply to the second objection: though that God exists can be demonstrated simpliciter, that God is three and one and other things faith holds about God cannot, and it is in respect of these that 'believing God' is an act of faith.
claims: God's existence is demonstrable, but the Trinity and similar truths are not, and these are the object of faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e350.summary: Reply to the third objection: the believer believes a human not as human but as one in whom God speaks, which can be gathered from certain evidences. The unbeliever does not believe God speaking in a human.
claims: The believer trusts a human messenger only as one through whom God speaks.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e354.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: loving simpliciter is the act of charity, but believing lovingly is an act of faith moved by charity to its act.
claims: Believing lovingly is an act of faith moved by charity.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e357.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: the four phrases belong to faith as ordered to the will, whose object is the end, so they are distinguished by what is required to attain the end. First, affection for the end (believing lovingly); then motion toward it from love and desire (believing, to go into him); then union with the end (believing, to adhere to him); and from union, participation in the end's perfections (believing, to be incorporated into his members).
claims: The four phrases describe successive stages of reaching the end: affection, motion, union and participation.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e366.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: certainty is the intellect's determination to one, and it is greater as its cause is stronger. In understanding, determination comes from the evidence of what is seen by intellectual light; in science, from resolving conclusions into self-evident principles; in faith, from the will's command. The will does not make the believed visible but makes the intellect adhere firmly, so the certainty of science and understanding comes from evidence, and the certainty of faith from firmness of adherence. In faith the reason inclining the will is first truth itself, God, who is firmer than the light of human intellect or human reasoning. Hence faith has greater certainty in firmness of adherence than science or understanding, though they have greater evidence.
claims: Certainty is the intellect's determination to one and is greater as its cause is stronger.
The certainty of science and understanding derives from evidence; that of faith from firm adherence commanded by the will.
Because faith rests on first truth, it surpasses science in firmness of adherence, though science surpasses it in evidence.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e369.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith's certainty is between science and opinion not intensively, as on a continuous scale, but extensively, as by number. Science's certainty has two elements, evidence and firm adherence; faith's has one, firm adherence; opinion's has neither. Yet faith's one is stronger than science's two. Alternatively, Hugh speaks of faith as opinion strengthened by reasons, not infused faith.
claims: Faith is between science and opinion extensively, having one of science's two marks of certainty, but that mark is more intense in faith.
Hugh's dictum may refer to acquired opinion confirmed by reasons, not to infused faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e372.summary: Reply to the second objection: movements of doubt arise in the believer because the intellect is not terminated in vision but only by the will's command. In that respect the knower is further from doubt than the believer, but in firmness of adherence the believer is further from doubt than the knower in both respects.
claims: Movements of doubt in believers arise from lack of evidence, yet in firmness of adherence the believer surpasses the knower.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e375.summary: Reply to the third objection: the argument proceeds from an insufficient enumeration of the sources of certainty, since it omits the will's command.
claims: Certainty can also come from the will's command, not only from vision.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e394.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is faith in the will as subject?): Hugh of St Victor says faith has its matter in cognition but its substance in affection, and the subject of an accident is where its essence is. So faith's subject is the affect.
claims: Since faith's substance is in the affect, the affect is its subject.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e397.summary: Second objection: as the certainty of science comes from the intellect, the certainty of faith comes from the will, since no one believes unless willing. So as the intellect is the subject of science, the will is the subject of faith.
claims: The source of faith's certainty, the will, should be its subject.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e400.summary: Third objection: merit lies in the will, and the act of faith is meritorious. So it is an act of the will.
claims: Faith's meritorious act must belong to the will.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e403.summary: Fourth objection: opposites concern the same subject. Unbelief is in the will, since in the intellect it would be ignorance, which excuses rather than sins. So faith is in the will.
claims: Since culpable unbelief is in the will, faith is in the will.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e407.summary: Sed contra: a habit's object matches the object of its subject power. Faith's object is the true, which is the intellect's object, not the good, which is the will's. So faith's subject is the intellect.
claims: Since faith's object is the true, its subject is the intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e410.summary: Second sed contra: faith and what succeeds it in glory belong to the same power, and vision, which succeeds faith, belongs to the intellect.
claims: Faith belongs to the intellect, as does the vision that replaces it.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e419.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (does faith belong to the practical intellect?): the speculative intellect says nothing about what to avoid or love, but faith teaches what to avoid. So faith is in the practical intellect.
claims: Faith directs action and so belongs to the practical intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e422.summary: Second objection: the speculative intellect corresponds to imagination and the practical to estimation. Imagination produces neither confidence nor terror; yet faith is the principle of hope and causes trembling (the demons believe and tremble). So faith is not in the speculative intellect.
claims: Faith moves the affections, which the speculative intellect does not.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e425.summary: Third objection: the speculative intellect is not mixed with the will, but the practical is, and faith involves both intellect and will. So its subject is the practical intellect.
claims: Faith's involvement of the will places it in the practical intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e428.summary: Sed contra: the practical intellect concerns contingent things we can do, while faith concerns eternal things.
claims: Faith concerns eternal things and so is not in the practical intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e432.summary: Second sed contra: practical knowledge causes what it knows, but faith does not cause what it believes.
claims: Faith does not cause its objects and so is not practical knowledge.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e441.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (is faith an intellectual virtue?): an intellectual virtue has the intellect as subject, as faith does.
claims: Faith, having the intellect as subject, is an intellectual virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e444.summary: Second objection: the articles of faith are like principles of theology, and the understanding of principles is an intellectual virtue (Ethics VI). So faith in the articles is too.
claims: As the habit of principles is an intellectual virtue, so is faith in the articles.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e447.summary: Third objection: an intellectual virtue is one by which only truth is spoken, and nothing false can fall under faith.
claims: Faith never errs and so meets Aristotle's criterion for intellectual virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e450.summary: Sed contra: Aristotle says in Ethics VI that suspicion and opinion are not intellectual virtues, and faith belongs to their genus.
claims: Faith, like opinion, is not an intellectual virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e454.summary: Second sed contra: virtue brings a power to its ultimate (De caelo I), but faith does not, since through it the intellect is not terminated in any vision.
claims: Faith does not bring the intellect to its ultimate, vision, and so is not an intellectual virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e464.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1: the will commands the intellect's act, as it commands the irascible and concupiscible. For the latter's acts to be perfect, a habit is needed not only in the commanding will or reason but also in the executing powers, so that they carry out the act easily. So too a habit must be in the intellect for it to obey the will easily in matters above reason. That habit is faith, and its subject is the intellect.
claims: As the executing powers need habits to obey the will readily, the intellect needs the habit of faith to obey the will in matters above reason.
The subject of faith is the intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e467.summary: Reply to the first objection: 'substance' in Hugh means form, not essence, and the form of faith in a way is charity, which is in the will.
claims: Charity, in the will, is in a sense the form of faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e470.summary: Reply to the second objection: science and understanding derive certainty from something cognitive, the evidence of what is assented to, so they are in the power from which they derive certainty. Faith derives its certainty from something outside the genus of cognition, in affection, and so is not in the power from which its certainty comes.
claims: Faith's certainty comes from the affective order, but its subject remains the intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e473.summary: Reply to the third objection: merit lies in the will as cause, since the will is always involved in a meritorious act, but not always as subject, since meritorious acts are sometimes elicited by other powers.
claims: The will causes merit but is not always the subject of meritorious acts.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e477.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: unbelief is in the intellect as subject and in the will as commanding the act of unbelief, which makes it demeritorious.
claims: Unbelief is in the intellect as subject and in the will as cause of its culpability.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e486.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: speculative and practical intellect differ in that the former considers truth absolutely and the latter as ordered to action. Some truths cannot be rules of action (mathematics, things separated from motion) and belong to the speculative intellect alone. Others can, and then the speculative intellect becomes practical by extension. Some of these, being contingent, are valuable mainly as ordered to action, like the works of virtue, and so belong principally to the practical intellect. Others have dignity in themselves even apart from action, like divine things, which nonetheless direct action, since the vision of God is the last end of action. These belong principally to the speculative intellect and secondarily to the practical. Faith's proper object is first truth, which as the end of action regulates action, so faith is principally in the speculative intellect and secondarily in the practical. These are not two powers but differ by end.
claims: Speculative and practical intellect are one power differing by end, truth considered absolutely or as ordered to action.
Truths about divine things have dignity in themselves but also regulate action, since the vision of God is the end of all action.
Faith is principally in the speculative intellect and secondarily in the practical.
concepts: prima veritas as rule of action
vision of God as last end

ta-l3d23q2-d1e489.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith inclines to doing and avoiding insofar as the truth that can be considered in itself is taken as a rule of action.
claims: Faith guides action by taking speculative truth as a rule of action.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e492.summary: Reply to the second objection: insofar as the truth faith considers is taken as fitting or contrary, faith produces trembling or hope.
claims: Faith causes hope or fear when its truth is apprehended as fitting or harmful.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e495.summary: Reply to the third objection: what makes the intellect practical is not its conjunction with the will but its ordering to action. The will is common to both, since it concerns the end, and an end is found in both speculative and practical intellect.
claims: Ordering to action, not conjunction with the will, makes the intellect practical.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e504.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: since virtue brings a power to its ultimate in act, it is not enough that the power reach its ultimate as to object; it must also reach it as to mode, so that the act is not only of something good but done well, as in moral virtue. The intellect's good is truth. An intellectual virtue must therefore make one understand well, which comes not from good will but from the intellect's own efficacy in seeing its object, either in itself or by resolution to what is seen in itself. Faith brings the intellect to its ultimate as to object, by assent to first truth, but not as to the intellect's proper mode, since faith does not make the intellect able to see what it believes or reduce it to what it sees. So faith is not an intellectual virtue.
claims: A virtue must perfect a power in its mode of acting as well as in its object.
Intellectual virtue requires the intellect's own efficacy in seeing truth, not just good will.
Faith perfects the intellect as to object but not as to mode, and so is not an intellectual virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e507.summary: Reply to the first objection: not every habit in the intellect is an intellectual virtue, but only one that perfects it both as to object and as to mode of act.
claims: An intellectual virtue perfects the intellect in both object and mode.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e510.summary: Reply to the second objection: the agent intellect's light suffices to see the principles of other sciences, so their habit is a virtue. But neither the agent intellect's light nor the light of faith suffices to see the articles, so faith is not an intellectual virtue.
claims: Unlike first principles, the articles of faith are not seen by any light available in this life.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e513.summary: Reply to the third objection: faith's infallibility comes not from a perfect mode of understanding but from something outside the intellect, the infallible reason that directs the will.
claims: Faith's infallibility derives from the divine testimony moving the will, not from intellectual insight.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e531.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is faith a virtue?): no virtue except an intellectual one has truth as object or is cognitive rather than operative. Faith is cognitive and concerns truth but is not an intellectual virtue, so it is no virtue at all.
claims: Faith, cognitive but not intellectual virtue, cannot be a virtue at all.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e534.summary: Second objection: 'believing' is used univocally when we believe other people, and faith in others is not a virtue. So neither is faith in the articles.
claims: Belief in God and belief in humans are univocal, and the latter is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e537.summary: Third objection: whatever is against reason is blameworthy (Dionysius). Faith makes one renounce reason and so seems against reason, so believing is blameworthy and not a virtue.
claims: Faith requires renouncing reason and so is vicious.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e540.summary: Fourth objection: prophecy, like faith, knows what is above reason, and prophecy is not a virtue. So neither is faith.
claims: Prophecy and faith both know the supra-rational, and prophecy is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e544.summary: Fifth objection: virtues have exemplars in God, but faith has none. So faith is not a virtue.
claims: Faith lacks a divine exemplar and so is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e547.summary: Sed contra: only virtue justifies, and faith justifies (Romans 5:1).
claims: Faith justifies and so is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e558.summary: Second sed contra: spiritual life is through virtue, and it is through faith (Romans 1).
claims: Spiritual life comes through faith, so faith is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e561.summary: Third sed contra: we become children of God through virtues, and this happens through faith (John 1:12).
claims: Becoming God's children through faith shows that faith is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e578.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (is faith one virtue?): some articles concern eternal things (the Trinity), others temporal things (the Incarnation), and knowledge and wisdom are different gifts because they concern temporal and eternal things. So faith is not one virtue.
claims: Articles about eternal and temporal things require distinct habits.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e581.summary: Second objection: hope and fear differ as concerning future goods and evils, and faith concerns both rewards and punishments. So faith is not one virtue.
claims: Faith concerns both goods and evils and so should be divided.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e584.summary: Third objection: faith includes matters belonging to moral philosophy (fornication is mortal sin), natural philosophy (the world is not eternal), and first philosophy (God cares for human acts). So faith is not one habit.
claims: Faith's matter spans several sciences and so cannot be one habit.
Scripture affirms one faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e599.summary: Second sed contra: faith directs intention in matters of grace as prudence does in political matters (Augustine), and prudence is one though it directs in many things.
claims: Like prudence, faith is one though it directs many things.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e608.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1: an operation is good formally, as proceeding from a power moved to the good as good, or materially, as suited to its power. The act of faith is good in both ways: it suits the intellect as concerning truth, and it proceeds from the commanding will, moved to the good as object. On the intellect's side it lacks perfection of mode, since the truth it adheres to is not evident. On the will's side it can be perfect, since a will perfect in desire of the good gives faith firmness and certainty, which is why Bernard calls faith 'a voluntary and certain foretaste of truth not yet disclosed'. So faith is a virtue, not intellectual, but in the common sense of a habit producing a good act from the goodness of the will. Nor is it moral, since it does not order sense appetite about pleasures, pains and operations. It is a theological virtue, a genus the philosophers did not know.
claims: The act of faith is good both materially, as concerning truth, and formally, as commanded by a will moved to the good.
Faith is perfect on the will's side, which gives it firmness and certainty, though imperfect in its intellectual mode.
Faith is neither an intellectual nor a moral virtue but a theological virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e614.summary: Reply to the first objection: the premise is true of the virtues the philosophers knew, who posited none besides intellectual and moral virtues.
claims: The philosophers knew only intellectual and moral virtues.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e617.summary: Reply to the second objection: the reason that inclines the will to believe the articles is first truth itself, which is infallible. The reason that inclines it to believe other things is a fallible sign or the word of someone who can deceive or be deceived. So the will does not give infallible truth to belief in other matters, and only faith in the articles is a virtue.
claims: Faith in the articles rests on infallible first truth, while human belief rests on fallible testimony, so only the former is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e620.summary: Reply to the third objection: faith is not against reason but above it. It renounces reason not by destroying true reason but by bringing it into captivity to the obedience of Christ (2 Corinthians 10).
claims: Faith is above reason, not against it, and captivates reason without destroying it.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e624.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: prophecy can in no way be a virtue. It is not intellectual, since what it reveals cannot be resolved into naturally known principles; not theological, since its object is temporal things, not God; and the prophet's intellectual act is not commanded by the will.
claims: Prophecy is not a virtue: it is neither intellectual nor theological, and it is not commanded by the will.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e627.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: faith has an exemplar in God as to what is perfect in it, knowledge and certainty, but not as to its imperfection, and its being a virtue does not come from that imperfection.
claims: Faith's perfections of knowledge and certainty have exemplars in God.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e637.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: habits are one or many by their object, and faith's object is first truth, simple and unchangeable. So faith has a double unity. Because what it rests on is one and simple, the habit is not divided into many habits in the believer. Because it is truth, it unites different believers in the likeness of one faith, through the same thing believed, since truth gathers and unites, while error and ignorance divide (Dionysius).
claims: The habit of faith is one in each believer because its object, first truth, is simple.
Faith unites many believers in one faith because truth is unifying.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e640.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith does not have anything temporal as its object, but temporal things fall under it as they relate to eternal truth, as faith believes the passion insofar as God suffered.
claims: Temporal articles fall under faith insofar as they pertain to God.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e643.summary: Reply to the second objection: hope and fear belong to the affect, whose object is good and evil, and so they differ by good and evil. But good and evil do not differ under the ratio of truth, so faith, whose object is the true, is not divided by its concerning both.
claims: Good and evil do not differ under the ratio of truth, so faith remains one.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e646.summary: Reply to the third objection: faith considers all those diverse matters under one ratio, as they rest on first truth. So it is not diversified by them, though the sciences that consider them under their proper rationes are diverse.
claims: Faith considers all its matters under the single ratio of first truth.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e659.summary: First objection: all virtues are infused together, and of things that are simultaneous none is after another. So faith is not prior.
claims: Since virtues are infused simultaneously, none is prior.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e662.summary: Second objection: a foundation is the first part of a building. A gloss calls fortitude the foundation of faith, Bernard says the virtues are founded in humility, and 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom'. So faith is not first.
claims: Fortitude, humility and fear are each called foundations, so faith is not first.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e679.summary: Third objection: the theological virtues order a person to the end, and hope and charity are nearer the end than faith, having it as object under the ratio of end. So they are prior.
claims: Hope and charity, being nearer the end, are prior to faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e683.summary: Fourth objection: a gloss on Psalm 36 says hope leads into faith. So hope is prior.
claims: Hope leads to faith and so precedes it.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e689.summary: Fifth objection: the order of habits follows the order of powers. Faith is in the intellect as moved by the will, and charity is in the will, so charity is prior to faith.
claims: As the will moves the intellect in belief, charity in the will is prior to faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e692.summary: Sixth objection: faith is principally in the speculative intellect, and the contemplative life follows the active, since the mind must first be purified by action. So the moral virtues of the active life are prior to faith.
claims: The moral virtues of the active life precede the contemplative faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e695.summary: Sed contra: knowledge precedes affection, since nothing is loved unless known (Augustine). Faith is cognitive and the other virtues affective, so faith is prior.
claims: Faith, as cognitive, precedes the affective virtues.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e698.summary: Second sed contra: all virtues require right intention, and faith directs intention (Augustine).
claims: Faith directs the intention required by every virtue.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e701.summary: Third sed contra: through all virtues one approaches God, and whoever approaches God must believe (Hebrews 11).
claims: Every approach to God presupposes faith.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e705.summary: Aquinas's determination: priority is of time or of nature. In time all the virtues are simultaneous, being infused together. By nature their order follows their acts, as with the powers concreated in the soul. The act of faith is knowledge of truth, which the affection for the good required in all other virtues presupposes. So faith, as such, is naturally prior to all the other virtues.
claims: All virtues are infused simultaneously, but by nature faith is prior.
Faith is naturally first because the knowledge of truth it provides is presupposed by every affection for the good.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e708.summary: Reply to the first objection: it concerns the order of time.
claims: The objection concerns temporal, not natural, priority.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e711.summary: Reply to the second objection: 'foundation' is used metaphorically and can refer to order (the foundation precedes) or to strength (it supports the building). Faith is a foundation in both senses, being naturally first and the support of the others, since without faith it is impossible to please God. Fortitude is a foundation in the second sense, making the spiritual building firm against adversity; humility against prosperity, the occasion of sin; and fear against sin itself, so fear precedes the other affective virtues, introducing charity.
claims: Faith is a foundation both by priority and by support.
Fortitude, humility and fear are foundations only in the sense of securing the spiritual edifice against particular dangers.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e717.summary: Reply to the third objection: hope and charity are nearer the end in attainment, since charity in a sense reaches the end, but they are not therefore prior by nature. They follow faith, which shows them the end.
claims: Hope and charity are nearer the end in attainment but follow faith, which shows them the end.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e720.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: as the end is first in intention and last in being, what is nearer the end is prior in intention though posterior in being. Hope precedes faith in intention, not in being. When eternal goods are proposed, one first wills them, then wills to cleave to them in love, then to hope for them, and then to believe them, so that believing one can hope, love and possess. In being, faith is first.
claims: Hope precedes faith in intention but faith precedes hope in being.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e723.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: faith presupposes the will, not as already loving but as intending to love. The affect cannot be made firm in love where the intellect is not made firm by assent, just as it cannot desire what the intellect has not apprehended. The natural order is: God is apprehended (cogitation preceding faith), then one wills to reach him, then wills to love, and so on.
claims: Faith presupposes a will intending to love, not an already loving will.
Affection cannot be firm in what the intellect has not firmly assented to.

ta-l3d23q2-d1e727.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: faith does not belong only to the contemplative life. It is the principle of both active and contemplative life, since it shows the end of each.
claims: Faith is the principle of both the active and the contemplative life.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e243.summary: Objections to the first quaestiuncula, whether believing is 'to think with assent' (Augustine). They argue that assent belongs to the will, that faith is non-inquisitive, that cogitation is a sensitive act, and that the formula also fits science.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e261.summary: Objections to the second quaestiuncula, whether the act of faith is rightly multiplied into believing God, believing God's word, and believing in God. They argue that one habit has one act, that God's existence is demonstrable, that even unbelievers grant God speaks truly, that love belongs to charity, and that Lombard's fourfold phrasing is redundant.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e283.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether faith is less certain than science. The objections cite Hugh's 'below science', faith's admission of doubt, and the dependence of certainty on vision. The sed contra cites Augustine and the infinitely greater firmness of the divine reason behind faith.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e306.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula: an analysis of assent. Faith belongs to the intellect's composing and dividing. The intellect is determined to one side either by evidence (understanding), by resolution to principles (science), or by the will's command (belief), while opinion, doubt and ignorance fall short of assent. Believing alone combines assent with ongoing cogitation, since the intellect is determined from outside by the will. The replies distinguish assent (intellect) from consent (will), place faith between a preceding cogitation that inclines the will and a concomitant one seeking understanding, and locate the cogitative power at the border of sense and intellect.
claims: Belief is assent caused by the will's command, combined with continuing cogitation because the intellect is not terminated by evidence.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e336.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula: the act of faith depends on the intellect terminated to one (credere Deum), the will commanding it (credere in Deum, tending by love), and the reason moving the will, namely that God says it (credere Deo). These name one act under three aspects. The replies explain that the Trinity, unlike God's existence, is not demonstrable; that one believes humans only as God speaks in them; that believing lovingly is faith moved by charity; and that the fourfold phrasing traces the stages of reaching the end: affection, motion, union, incorporation.
claims: Credere Deum, credere Deo and credere in Deum name one act of faith under the aspects of intellect, motive and will.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e361.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula: certainty is the intellect's determination to one. In science and understanding it comes from evidence, in faith from firm adherence commanded by the will on account of first truth. So faith exceeds science in firmness, though not in evidence. Faith stands between science and opinion only extensively, having one of science's two marks of certainty, and movements of doubt arise from its lack of evidence.
claims: Faith is more certain than science in firmness of adherence, less in evidence.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e389.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether faith is in the will as subject. The objections appeal to Hugh's 'substance in the affect', to the will as source of faith's certainty, to merit's residence in the will, and to unbelief as a voluntary fault. The sed contra argues from faith's object, the true, and from vision as faith's successor in the intellect.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e414.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether faith belongs to the practical intellect. The objections note that faith teaches what to avoid, moves to hope and fear, and involves the will. The sed contra replies that faith concerns eternal things and does not cause its objects.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e436.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether faith is an intellectual virtue. The objections argue from its subject, from the analogy of the articles to first principles, and from its infallibility. The sed contra groups faith with opinion and notes that it does not bring the intellect to vision.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e459.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula: as executing powers need habits to obey the will readily, the intellect needs the habit of faith to obey the will in matters above reason, so the intellect is faith's subject. The replies interpret Hugh's 'substance' as form, namely charity in the will; explain that faith's certainty comes from the affective order without making the will its subject; and distinguish the will as cause of merit and of the culpability of unbelief from the subject of the act.
claims: The subject of faith is the intellect, made ready by faith to obey the will in what exceeds reason.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e481.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula: speculative and practical intellect are one power differing by end. Divine truths have dignity in themselves and also regulate action, since the vision of God is the last end. So faith is principally in the speculative intellect and secondarily in the practical. The replies explain how faith guides action, moves hope and fear, and why conjunction with the will does not make it practical.
claims: Faith is principally speculative and secondarily practical.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e499.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula: a virtue must perfect its power in both object and mode. Faith attains first truth as object but does not give the intellect the power to see it or resolve it into what is seen. So faith is not an intellectual virtue. Its infallibility comes from the divine witness moving the will, and the articles, unlike first principles, are seen by no light available in via.
claims: Faith is not an intellectual virtue because it perfects the intellect in object but not in mode.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e526.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether faith is a virtue. The objections argue that a cognitive non-intellectual habit cannot be a virtue, that belief in God is univocal with belief in humans, that faith renounces reason, that it parallels prophecy, and that it lacks a divine exemplar. The sed contra cites faith's role in justification, spiritual life and divine sonship.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e573.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether faith is one virtue. The objections cite its eternal and temporal articles, its concern with goods and evils, and its overlap with several sciences. The sed contra cites 'one faith' and the analogy with prudence.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e603.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula: the act of faith is materially good, as concerning truth, and formally good, as commanded by a will moved to the good, and it is perfected on the will's side, which gives it firmness. So faith is a virtue, neither intellectual nor moral but theological. The replies distinguish faith in the articles, which rests on infallible first truth, from fallible human belief. They hold that faith is above reason, not against it, deny that prophecy is a virtue, and locate faith's exemplar in God's knowledge and certainty.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue, good through the will's command and resting on infallible first truth.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e632.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula: faith is one because its object, first truth, is simple. That makes the habit undivided in each believer and, since truth unites, makes all believers one in faith. Temporal articles fall under faith as relating to God, good and evil do not differ under the ratio of truth, and faith considers diverse sciences' matters under the single ratio of first truth.
claims: Faith is one habit in each believer and one faith among believers, by reason of its simple object, first truth.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e103.summary: Prooemium of the question on faith, announcing five articles: what faith is, its act, its subject, whether it is a virtue, and its order to the other virtues.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e112.summary: Article 1 defends the Apostle's definition of faith (Hebrews 11:1) against eight objections. Aquinas holds that it is a proper definition in content, since a habit is known through its act, which is specified by object and made good by end. 'Argument of things not appearing' gives faith's object, God as first truth beyond natural intellect. 'Substance of things to be hoped for' gives its end, God as a good beyond human power yet freely self-communicating. 'Substance' means foundation of the spiritual edifice. 'Argument' means a foretaste of future vision and an infused light manifesting the articles. Faith is of things 'not appearing', not 'doubtful', because it lacks vision but not firm adherence. The affective part comes first because belief proceeds from the will. Finally, Aquinas shows that the definitions of Damascene, Dionysius, Augustine and Hugh of St Victor are all contained in the Apostle's.
claims: The Apostle's definition defines faith through its object (first truth not appearing) and its end (the good hoped for).
Faith is the foundation of the spiritual life and a foretaste of the vision to come.
Faith lacks vision but not firmness, so it is of things not apparent rather than doubtful.
All other patristic and scholastic definitions of faith are contained in the Apostle's.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e235.summary: Article 2 analyses the act of faith in three quaestiunculae. First, it defends Augustine's 'thinking with assent' through an account of the determination of the intellect. Understanding is determined by evidence, science by resolution to principles, and belief by the will's command, moved by a reason insufficient to terminate the intellect. So the believer alone has assent together with ongoing cogitation, faith 'captivates' the intellect, and faith stands between a cogitation that inclines the will and one that seeks understanding. Second, it explains the triad credere Deum, credere Deo and credere in Deum as one act seen from the side of intellect, motive (God's testimony) and will, with Lombard's fourfold phrasing mapping the stages of reaching the end. Third, it argues that faith is more certain than science in firmness of adherence, because it rests on first truth, though less certain in evidence.
claims: Belief is assent caused by the will's command on account of divine testimony, and it is accompanied by continuing cogitation.
Credere Deum, credere Deo and credere in Deum are aspects of one act of faith.
Faith exceeds science in firmness of adherence but not in evidence.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e381.summary: Article 3 locates the subject of faith. Faith is in the intellect, not the will. Just as the executing powers need habits to obey the will readily, the intellect needs faith to obey the will's command in matters above reason. Charity, in the will, is in a sense faith's form, and the will is the source of faith's certainty and merit without being its subject. Within the intellect, faith is principally speculative and secondarily practical, since its object, first truth, has dignity in itself but also regulates action as the last end. Yet faith is not an intellectual virtue: it reaches its object but not the intellect's proper mode of seeing, and its infallibility comes from the divine witness, not from insight.
claims: The subject of faith is the intellect, perfected to obey the will in what is above reason.
Faith is principally in the speculative intellect and secondarily in the practical.
Faith is not an intellectual virtue because it does not perfect the intellect's proper mode of seeing.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e518.summary: Article 4 shows that faith is a virtue and that it is one. Its act is materially good, concerning truth, and formally good, proceeding from a will moved to the good. Though imperfect in intellectual mode, it is perfected on the side of the will, which gives it firmness. So it is a virtue, not intellectual or moral but theological, a genus unknown to the philosophers. Faith in the articles is a virtue because its motive, first truth, is infallible, unlike fallible human belief. It is above reason, not against it, and prophecy is no virtue. Faith is one because its object, first truth, is simple: the habit is undivided in each believer and unites all believers in one faith, while the diverse matters it covers are held under the single ratio of first truth.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue, made good and firm by the will moved to the good and resting on infallible first truth.
Faith is one, in each believer and among believers, because its formal object, first truth, is one and simple.

ta-l3d23q2-Dd1e651.summary: Article 5 argues that faith is naturally prior to the other virtues, though all are infused at once. The order of virtues follows their acts, and every affection for the good presupposes the knowledge of truth that faith supplies. The replies interpret the 'foundation' metaphor: faith is a foundation by order and support, while fortitude, humility and fear secure the edifice against adversity, prosperity and sin. Hope and charity are nearer the end in attainment and hope precedes faith in intention, but faith precedes them in being. Faith presupposes a will intending, not already exercising, love, and it is the principle of both active and contemplative life.
claims: All virtues are infused simultaneously, but faith is naturally prior because knowledge precedes affection.
Hope may precede faith in intention, but faith precedes hope and charity in being.

ta-l3d23q2.summary: The second question of Distinction 23 treats faith in itself, in five articles. Article 1 defends Hebrews 11:1 as a proper definition, giving faith's object (first truth, not appearing) and end (the good hoped for). Faith is the foundation of the spiritual life and a foretaste of vision, and the other classical definitions are contained in it. Article 2 analyses belief as assent caused not by evidence but by the will's command, on account of God's testimony. The believer has assent together with ongoing cogitation, the triad credere Deum, Deo and in Deum names one act, and faith exceeds science in firmness of adherence though not in evidence. Article 3 places faith in the intellect, principally speculative, as the habit that makes the intellect obey the will in what exceeds reason. It is not an intellectual virtue, since it does not perfect the intellect's mode of seeing. Article 4 shows that faith is nonetheless a virtue, a theological one, perfected through the will and resting on infallible first truth, and that it is one because its object is simple. Article 5 makes faith naturally prior to all other virtues, because knowledge precedes affection. The question gives a sustained account of faith as a will-moved, intellect-located, supernatural assent to first truth.
claims: Faith is defined through its object, first truth not seen, and its end, the good hoped for.
Belief is assent caused by the will on account of divine testimony, firmer than science though lacking evidence.
Faith resides in the intellect, chiefly the speculative, but is a theological, not an intellectual, virtue.
Faith is one because its formal object, first truth, is simple.
Faith is naturally prior to the other virtues.
